q: What structural system did Egyptian architecture use?
n: Egyptian architecture was columnar and trabeated: massive columns and walls carrying stone beams and roof slabs. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Egyptian architecture).

q: Which style has battered walls, no windows and gorge cornices?
n: Battered (sloping) walls, the absence of windows and gorge (cavetto) cornices are all hallmarks of Egyptian architecture. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which civilization built structures on platforms 6 to 10 meters high, with a conical shape and pipe holes?
n: West Asiatic (Mesopotamian) builders raised ziggurats and palaces on platforms about 6–10 m high, with drainage holes, to escape floods. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (West Asiatic architecture).

q: What type of column is characterized by a lotus or papyrus capital, commonly found in Egyptian architecture?
n: The lotiform column has a capital in the shape of a lotus bud or flower. Papyriform and palmiform columns imitate other Nile plants. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Egyptian columns).

q: What is the columned hall of an Egyptian temple, meant to suggest a papyrus marsh, called?
n: A hypostyle hall is a hall whose roof rests on many columns. In Egyptian temples it evoked a papyrus marsh. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which Roman building still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome?
n: The Pantheon's dome (about 43.3 m) is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; MacDonald, The Pantheon.

q: What is the largest surviving Roman triumphal arch, finished in AD 315?
n: The Arch of Constantine (AD 315), beside the Colosseum, is the largest surviving Roman triumphal arch. It commemorates the victory at the Milvian Bridge. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which was the largest Roman circus and one of the biggest arenas ever built?
n: The Circus Maximus in Rome was the largest Roman circus, holding about 150,000 spectators for chariot races. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Who began the construction of the Great Hypostyle Hall in the Temple of Karnak?
n: Seti I began the Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak and Ramesses II completed it. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; UNESCO (Ancient Thebes).

q: What were Roman aqueducts for?
n: Roman aqueducts carried and distributed water to cities by gravity, using channels on arcades and in tunnels. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: How did the Egyptians make a level base for the pyramids?
o: By cutting trenches, filling them with water and marking the waterline
n: The Egyptians leveled pyramid bases by cutting a grid of trenches, filling them with water and marking the waterline, which is naturally level. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Arnold, Building in Egypt.

q: What method was used to transfer 2-ton stones during the construction of the pyramids?
o: Lifted them one by one on top of the other
Used rolled logs to move and position them
n: Large stones were moved on sledges, rollers (logs) and ramps, then levered into position. Source: Arnold, Building in Egypt: Pharaonic Stone Masonry.

q: Who was chief architect of the Great Pyramid of Giza?
n: Hemiunu, Khufu's vizier, is credited as the architect of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Hemiunu; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the name of the ancient stone figure with the body of a lion and the head of a human?
n: A sphinx has the body of a lion and the head of a human, like the Great Sphinx of Giza. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Who designed the Step Pyramid of Zoser?
n: Imhotep designed the Step Pyramid of Zoser (Djoser) at Saqqara, the first monumental stone building. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which architect was deified and honored during the reign of Rameses?
n: Imhotep was later deified and honored as a god of medicine and wisdom in later dynasties. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Imhotep.

q: What is the pool in Egyptian temples used for ritual purification called?
n: Egyptian temples had a sacred lake, a stone-lined pool used by priests for ritual purification, as at Karnak. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What massive gateway fronted Egyptian temples, carved and often flanked by obelisks?
n: A pylon is the monumental gateway of twin tapering towers fronting an Egyptian temple, carved with reliefs and often flanked by obelisks. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What tall, four-sided tapering monument symbolized the sun god Ra?
n: The obelisk, a tall four-sided tapering monolith, symbolized the sun god Ra, and its gilded tip caught the first light. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What was the prototype of the Egyptian pyramid?
n: The mastaba was the prototype of the pyramid. Stacking mastabas produced Zoser's step pyramid. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: In Roman work, opus tessellatum is:
n: Opus tessellatum is Roman mosaic of small, regular cubes (tesserae) set in mortar. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which Roman wall facing forms a net-like diagonal pattern?
n: Opus reticulatum is Roman wall facing of square stones set diagonally, forming a net-like pattern (reticulum means net). Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What was the warm room of a Roman bath?
n: The tepidarium was the warm room of a Roman bath, between the frigidarium (cold) and caldarium (hot). Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Roman thermae).

q: What was the sweating room of a Roman bath?
n: The sudatorium (sudarium) was the sweating room of a Roman bath (sudor means sweat). Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What were the bedrooms of a Roman domus called?
n: The bedrooms of a Roman domus were cubicula (singular cubiculum), opening off the atrium. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Roman houses).

q: What is the triangular gable above the entablature?
n: The pediment is the triangular gable above the entablature at the ends of a temple roof. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Where is the pediment on a Doric temple?
n: On a Doric temple the pediment sits above the entablature, on the cornice, at each gable end. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What does the pediment of a Classical temple hold?
o: The tympanum, often filled with mythological sculpture
n: The pediment encloses the tympanum, often filled with sculpture groups from mythology. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is a wide, low-pitched gable over a colonnade or a main section of a façade?
n: A pediment is the wide, low-pitched triangular gable crowning a portico or the main section of a facade. The tympanum is only its inner field. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: In Greek temples, the cella is also called the:
n: The cella of a Greek temple is also called the naos: the inner sanctuary that held the cult statue. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: The Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae is also known as the:
n: The Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae, a large tholos (beehive) tomb, is also called the Tomb of Agamemnon. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Aegean architecture).

q: Where did the agora originate?
n: The agora originated in Greece as the open public marketplace and assembly place of the city. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What was the long colonnaded hall of Greek cities?
n: The stoa was a long colonnaded hall lining the Greek agora, giving shelter for commerce and conversation. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What open, colonnaded building, often very long, served as a public meeting place?
n: A stoa is an open, colonnaded and often very long building that served as a public meeting place. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Who was the Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BC?
n: Vitruvius, a Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BC, wrote De architectura (Ten Books on Architecture). Source: Vitruvius, De architectura; Encyclopaedia Britannica.

q: What was the Colosseum mainly for?
n: The Colosseum was built mainly for public entertainment: gladiator games, animal hunts and spectacles. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the effect of using a rib vault in architecture?
n: Rib vaults concentrate thrust on the ribs and piers, freeing the walls between to be opened for larger windows, the basis of Gothic glass walls. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (Gothic construction).

q: Which temple has a circular plan under a dome about 142 ft across, praised by Jefferson as a model of the spherical arch?
n: The Pantheon has a circular plan under a dome about 142 ft across. Jefferson called it a model of the spherical arch and copied it for the University of Virginia Rotunda. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; University of Virginia history.

q: What is the total height of the Pantheon in Rome?
n: The Pantheon's dome is 43.3 m (about 142 ft) in both diameter and height, so a perfect sphere fits inside the rotunda. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; MacDonald, The Pantheon.

q: Which Egyptian temple at Thebes is known for its grand colonnades and obelisk?
n: Luxor Temple at Thebes is known for its grand colonnade and the obelisk at its entrance (its twin is in Paris). Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture; UNESCO (Ancient Thebes).

q: What stone was mainly used to build Luxor Temple?
n: Luxor Temple was built mainly of Nubian sandstone quarried at Gebel el-Silsila. Source: Arnold, Building in Egypt; UNESCO (Ancient Thebes).

q: Luxor Temple wasn't built for a cult god's daily rites. It was dedicated to:
n: Luxor Temple was dedicated to the renewal (rejuvenation) of kingship, celebrated in the Opet festival. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Luxor; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Whatconstruction system was employed in the construction of the Parthenon?
n: The Parthenon is trabeated: columns carrying lintels (post and lintel), the Greek system. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Which order was used for the Parthenon's peristyle?
n: The Parthenon's outer peristyle is Doric, with an Ionic frieze inside around the cella. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the name of Figure A?
n: Figure A is the Arch of Constantine, the triple-bay triumphal arch beside the Colosseum. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the name of Figure B?
n: Figure B is the Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis. The Parthenon (447–432 BC), by Ictinus and Callicrates, is the supreme Doric temple, dedicated to Athena. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the name of Figure C?
n: Figure C is the Pantheon in Rome, with its portico and domed rotunda. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the name of Figure D?
n: Figure D is the Circus Maximus, the long chariot-racing arena in Rome. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: What is the name of Figure E?
n: Figure E is the Erechtheion, on the Acropolis, with its caryatid porch. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture.
